answer.answer: This asks whether the university has a written, published way for people to ask what personal data it holds about them and how it uses it.
answer.whyItMatters: A university holds personal data on students, applicants, alumni, staff and parents, and many students may be children. People who gave consent can ask for a summary of their data and who it was shared with. A clear, published route helps the university answer such requests consistently.
answer.moreDetail: A Data Principal (the person the data is about, including a parent for a child) can ask a Data Fiduciary (here, the university, which decides why and how data is used) for three things: a summary of their personal data and how it is processed; the names of other organisations and vendors it was shared with, and what was shared; and any other information the Rules prescribe (s.11(1)). This right applies where the person gave consent, including where they voluntarily provided data for a specified purpose (s.7(a)). Where data is held on another legitimate use, such as employment of staff (s.7(i)), the access right does not apply in the same way. Which records fall where, for example admissions, examinations or hostel data, is for the university and counsel to confirm. The Rules require the university to publish prominently on its website or app how to make a request and what identifier it needs, such as an enrolment ID or application number (Rule 14(1), Rule 14(5)). Every response must give the contact of a person who can answer questions about the processing (Rule 9). These Rules apply from 13 May 2027. The law sets no deadline for answering an access request. TrustStack's target is thirty days, with ninety days as its outer limit; this is TrustStack's method, not the law. A reviewer decides whether any evidence you add meets the question.

answer.answer: No — consent needs a clear affirmative action by the person, and a pre-ticked box involves no such action, so it is unlikely to be enough.
answer.whyItMatters: A university collects personal data from students, applicants, alumni and staff through portals, forms and apps. Where any of that rests on consent, the university must be able to prove that consent was validly given. Pre-ticked boxes on admission or alumni forms would weaken that proof.
answer.moreDetail:
The Act says consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given with a clear affirmative action (s.6(1)). A clear affirmative action means the person does something positive, such as ticking an empty box or clicking 'I agree'. A box already ticked for them is not their action. Consent must also be limited to the data needed for the stated purpose (s.6(1)). So bundling unrelated uses, such as marketing alongside admissions, into one tick is also a risk.

The request for consent must come with, or after, a notice (a plain statement of what data is used and why) (s.5(1)). It must be in clear, plain language, with an option for English or a language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution (s.6(3)). Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it (s.6(4)). If ever questioned, the university, as Data Fiduciary (the body deciding why and how data is used), must prove the notice and consent (s.6(10)). That is why logs matter.

Not all university processing needs consent. Some may rest on another legitimate use under s.7, for example employment for staff (s.7(i)). Which basis applies to each activity is for the university and its counsel to confirm. The detailed notice requirements in Rule 3 apply from 13 May 2027.

When you answer, a reviewer decides whether any evidence you add supports it.

Processing for employment purposes is a legitimate use that does not rely on consent.

answer.answer: This question asks whether Mumbai University gives people a clear notice before, or at the same time as, it asks for their consent to collect personal data.
answer.whyItMatters: A university collects personal data at many points: admissions, enrolment, examinations, hostels, alumni and events. Many forms may also involve students under eighteen, which brings extra rules on parental consent.
answer.moreDetail: The Act says every request for consent must come with, or be preceded by, a notice from the Data Fiduciary (here, the university, which decides why and how personal data is used). The notice must tell the Data Principal (the person the data is about; for a child, this includes the parent or lawful guardian) what personal data is being collected and why, how to withdraw consent and raise a grievance, and how to complain to the Data Protection Board of India. The Rules add detail. The notice must stand on its own and use clear, plain language. It must itemise the data and describe the specific purpose and service. It must give a link to the website or app for withdrawing consent, exercising rights and complaining to the Board. People must be able to read it in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution, such as Marathi or Hindi. Where people consented before the Act began, the university must give them a notice as soon as reasonably practicable. Timing: Rule 3, which sets out the notice details, applies from 13 May 2027. The duty in the Act itself sits in s.5. Not every collection rests on consent. Some data may be processed for a 'legitimate use' under s.7, for example employment records of staff under s.7(i). Which collections need a consent notice is for the university and its counsel to confirm. To answer this question, list the main collection points: admission portals, enrolment and exam forms, hostel and library forms, alumni and event sign-ups. For each one, check whether a notice appears before or at the point of collection. A reviewer then decides whether the evidence you add is accepted.

answer.answer: Tell the Board without delay on becoming aware, then send a detailed report within seventy-two hours, unless the Board allows longer on written request.
answer.whyItMatters: A university holds personal data on many students, staff and applicants, including children's data where students are under eighteen. A playbook lets IT/Security and Legal act within the seventy-two hours rather than working it out under pressure. This question is mandatory and is not yet answered.
answer.moreDetail: A personal data breach means any unauthorised processing, or accidental disclosure, loss, alteration or destruction, that compromises personal data (s.2(u)). Your university is the Data Fiduciary, the body that decides why and how personal data is used. On becoming aware of a breach it must tell the Data Protection Board of India (the Board) in two stages. First, without delay, it sends a description of the breach: its nature, extent, timing, location and likely impact. Second, within seventy-two hours of becoming aware, it sends a fuller report. This covers updated details, the facts and reasons behind the breach, mitigation measures, any findings about who caused it, steps to prevent recurrence, and a report on the notices sent to affected people. The Board can allow a longer period if you ask in writing (Rule 7(2)). You must also tell each affected person without delay, in clear and plain words (Rule 7(1)). These breach Rules apply from 13 May 2027, so there is time to prepare. A DPDP-specific playbook would set out who decides that the clock has started, who drafts each notice, and how you would request an extension. TrustStack also sends breach-clock alerts when forty-eight hours and twelve hours remain. That is TrustStack's own target, not the law. Whether a given incident counts as a breach is for your team and counsel to decide. A reviewer decides whether any playbook you upload is accepted as evidence.

law.point: On an erasure request, the organisation must erase the personal data unless keeping it is necessary for the specified purpose or to comply with a law. Deciding that is a legal judgement for a person and counsel.

Data processed for another legitimate use, such as employment, is outside the s.12 right. The basis for the hostel and mess records must be confirmed.
Where erasure is due, the university must also make its Data Processors (vendors who process data for it, such as a mess caterer, if any) erase the data they were given.
Every response to a rights request must give the business contact of the Data Protection Officer, if any, or of a person who can answer questions about the processing.
Personal data, traffic data and processing logs must be kept for at least one year from the processing. This may affect what can be erased now, once the rule applies.

The person must use the university's grievance process before going to the Board. The grievance reply period must not exceed ninety days under Rule 14(3); that period is for grievances, not for this request.
TrustStack's target is to answer a rights request within thirty days, with ninety days as its outer limit. These are TrustStack's targets, not the law; the law sets no period for an erasure request.

answer.answer: This draft notice covers ten University purposes for counsel to check; how to withdraw consent and complain to the Board is added by TrustStack.

draft.title: Mumbai University: how we use your personal data, and the consent we ask for
draft.summary: Mumbai University runs admissions, teaching, examinations, student services, events and alumni activities. To do this, we use personal data, meaning information about you. This notice explains each purpose we ask your consent for, what it does for you and the data it needs. You can choose for each purpose separately. Where a student or applicant is under eighteen, we ask a parent or lawful guardian to give verifiable consent, meaning consent we take reasonable steps to check, on their behalf. You can read this notice in English or in any language listed in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.

purposes.title: Admissions
purposes.uses: Lets you apply online. We use the data to check your eligibility, verify your documents and keep you updated about your application. If the applicant is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent first.
dataItems: Previous academic records and mark sheets
Reservation category certificate, if you claim a category
Parent's or guardian's name and contact details

purposes.title: Examinations and results
purposes.uses: Registers you for examinations, lets us run them and publish your results, and handles any request you make for revaluation.

purposes.title: Student records and administration
purposes.uses: Keeps your student record up to date while you study with us, including your courses, attendance, fees and documents. If the student is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent first.
dataItems: Student profile (name, date of birth, photograph)
Documents you submit to the University

purposes.title: Online learning
purposes.uses: Gives you access to the University's online learning platform so you can follow courses, submit assignments, take part in discussions and see your grades.

purposes.title: Scholarships and fee concessions
purposes.uses: Lets us check whether you qualify for a scholarship or fee concession and pay any award into your bank account.
dataItems: Reservation category, if relevant to the scheme
Parent's or guardian's details, where the scheme needs them

purposes.title: Sharing records with affiliated colleges
purposes.uses: Lets the University and your affiliated college exchange the records needed to run your course, examinations and required reporting.
dataItems: Submissions made by your college about you

purposes.title: AI help assistant
purposes.uses: Lets you ask questions through an automated chat assistant and get answers about University services. The assistant is run by a computer program, not a person.
dataItems: Name and contact details, only if you choose to give them

purposes.title: Event and webinar registration
purposes.uses: Registers you for a University event or webinar and lets us send you joining details and updates about it.

purposes.title: Photographs at University events
purposes.uses: Lets us take photographs and video recordings at University events in which you may appear, and use them to show and record University activities.

purposes.title: Alumni updates
purposes.uses: Keeps you in touch with the University after you graduate, with news, invitations to alumni events and information about ways to support the University, including donations.

law.point: Every request for consent must come with or after a notice setting out the personal data, the purpose, and how to use rights and complain to the Board.
The notice must stand on its own, use clear and plain language, itemise the data and describe each purpose and what it provides. It applies from 13 May 2027.
Consent must be free, specific, informed and limited to the data needed for each purpose, so each purpose is offered separately.
Before processing a child's data, the University must obtain the verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian.
Sets how the University checks that the person giving consent for a child is an identifiable adult parent.
Some processing may rest on a legitimate use instead of consent; such purposes must not be presented as needing consent.
People must be able to read the notice in English or any Eighth Schedule language.

missingInformation: The lawful basis for every record is undecided. Counsel to confirm which purposes rest on consent and which on a legitimate use under s.7 (for example s.7(a), or s.7(c) if the University acts as a State instrumentality), and remove the latter from this notice.
Withdrawal, Board-complaint and contact wording is not in this draft by design; TrustStack prints it on every notice in fixed words.
Confirm which applicants and students may be under eighteen, and how parental verifiable consent will be checked under Rule 10.
Faculty data in the learning platform and affiliated college exchange may rest on employment under s.7(i). Counsel to confirm whether faculty need a separate notice.
Some data items are vague in the records ("documents", "profile", "category"). A person should list each item exactly.
For the AI help assistant, confirm whether chats are stored by a vendor or used to improve the system, and whether visitors who are children may use it.
For event photographs, confirm where images are published and whether consent is asked per event.
Confirm whether alumni donations involve payment details, which would need adding to that purpose.

draft.headline: The assessment is still provisional and evidence is thin: 4 artefacts are stored, a reviewer has rated 1 Adequate, and all 4 remediation actions are still outstanding.
paragraphs: This pack is dated 22 October 2026 and is provisional, because 123 questions in the 'Mumbai University DPDP Compass Baseline' are still unanswered. There are 203 days to 13 May 2027, when most of the DPDP Rules commence. The report shows 4 of 4 applicable penalty heads as exposed, partially mitigated or not yet assessed. Their statutory ceilings total ₹700 crore. That figure is a set of legal maximums under the Schedule to the Act, not a predicted fine.

Four artefacts (items of evidence) are stored. A reviewer has rated 1 Adequate and 1 Partial, and 2 are awaiting review. None is unlinked. Security safeguards (s.8(5)) and 'any other provision' each draw on 3 artefacts. Security safeguards is not yet assessed, and 'any other provision' is shown as exposed. Breach notification (s.8(6)) is partially mitigated but has 0 artefacts. Children and lawful guardians (s.9) is not yet assessed, with 0 artefacts. Significant Data Fiduciary duties (s.10) are marked not applicable.

By obligation area, only governance has evidence: 1 artefact, rated Partial, with an evidence confidence of 60% from the scoring engine. Notice, consent, rights, grievance, retention, accuracy, security and breach readiness have no artefacts yet. None of the 10 live processing records has evidence attached. The processing register's gaps have never been generated.

No remediation action has been closed, either on accepted evidence or on a reviewer's approval, and 4 are still outstanding. The Board weighs evidence of mitigation, and how promptly it was taken, under s.33(2)(e).
bullets: Answer the 123 unanswered baseline questions, so the assessment is no longer provisional.

law.point: The Data Fiduciary (the university, which decides why and how personal data is used) is responsible for meeting the Act and the Rules, including for processing its vendors do on its behalf.
After an inquiry, the Board may impose a monetary penalty up to the amounts in the Schedule. The ₹700 crore figure is a total of those ceilings, not a forecast.
When deciding a penalty, the Board considers whether mitigating action was taken and how timely and effective it was. This is why reviewed evidence matters.
The Board may inquire into whether a person is complying with the Act. This pack is prepared for such an inquiry, an auditor or a reviewer.
Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 (notice, security, breach intimation, retention, children, rights and more) come into force eighteen months after publication, on 13 May 2027.
The law's own time limit applies to grievances: a published period not exceeding the limit in this rule. The Act and the Rules set no period for access, correction or erasure requests.

The report lists 4 further obligation areas ('moreRows') that this draft could not see; a person should check them before printing.

Whether the university processes children's data, and so how s.9 applies, is not yet assessed; the organisation and counsel should confirm this.
